## Design

### 2026-10-30: In this entry: I read through the guide to see what I could actually do and how to develop these LED Matrices.

**1h**

In this entry: I read through the guide to see what I could actually do and how to develop these LED Matrices.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/f088fd49a69e51ec96d65812ea23e0b666bd2e9cd1be79799df2b5652b2ac814.png)

By reading the guide, I learnt how LED Matrices use multiplexing to make the system seem like multiple lights are on at the same time. However these are just done very quickly in succession.

In terms of practicality for me however, I learnt that I would need to get a controller to do this action for me rather than me having a cpu do this constantly.

In this I would need a MAX7219 Module and in the guide, I was suggested to use a 4 in one module for scrolling text.

I then came to the section of setting up the schematic and putting together the parts.

Stage 1: (Added the connection):

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/4a5baee2b3374bac8196097574df9800989a99ba21da65d538004e5f8437579a.png)

Stage 2: (Which micro-processor):

Now as a beginner in this stuff I was not very familiar with how to choose a microprocessor especially on a case by case basis so I went and asked AI on which microprocessor might suit this situation better:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/7f4293de0540077f07cd4cee55296ae1275e627973520cb3adc7c52e4164690d.png)

From AI I learnt quite a few things:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/36eda435b3d0399c076b3df9509e044bfaa9d9a74305e8ae898374259b0381be.png)

Firstly I learnt that if I were to use a MAX7219 Module that did all the multiplexing for me, then I would really only ever need 3 wires anyway just to account for the SPI (1 for DIN, 1 for CLK, 1 for CS).

Therefore as only 3 GPIOs were I needed I really did not need to fret over GPIO space as AI says and I also did not need to account for many things apart from the basic pins.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/df20eac43d537d9d03bf32a0d7442dfbbf6939b08ad353faa7cc10813ff72800.png)

It also recommended me the cheapest option which would be the XIAO RP2040 which would already have enough pins (only 3 anyway) but was way cheaper.

The only other significant difference was that I would not have bluetooth connection with the microcontroller. But considering how I was simply going to plug in the controller and then run programs through there, I was not ver concerned with this bluetooth connection for now.

Because of this, even though I was more familiar with the ESP32, since the RP2040 was cheaper, I might as well choose  that and learn a bit more about micro-controllers.

I went to check the actual pricing of the RP2040 anyway just to see what price range I was looking at and was happy to see this was way cheaper than the ESP32:

https://www.aliexpress.com/item/1005012441490478.html?spm=a2g0o.productlist.main.3.73db5b1bguHPYp&algo_pvid=225ef741-7227-48cb-bc4f-e628fb0abd9b&algo_exp_id=225ef741-7227-48cb-bc4f-e628fb0abd9b-2&pdp_ext_f=%7B%22order%22%3A%2220%22%2C%22eval%22%3A%221%22%2C%22fromPage%22%3A%22search%22%7D&pdp_npi=6%40dis%21GBP%219.97%214.19%21%21%2186.21%2136.21%21%400b15832917933926291124567e0fc9%2112000060277369819%21sea%21UK%210%21ABX%211%210%21n_tag%3A-29910%3Bd%3A81bca6e7%3Bm03_new_user%3A-29895&curPageLogUid=Z6F5EntnLm2I&utparam-url=scene%3Asearch%7Cquery_from%3A%7Cx_object_id%3A1005012441490478%7C_p_origin_prod%3A
![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/ec45facf03173d88393b8785f3a0f9e9103b196022da361a60f172c2487bac4a.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/ec45facf03173d88393b8785f3a0f9e9103b196022da361a60f172c2487bac4a.png)

Out of curiosity in electronics I went and asked AI what made microcontrollers different so I would know what to do for future projects:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/3c0b2b15450eb13af4964d08a0420e328f1cd8730fd5b8800e7298c0b0731f91.png)

Through this I then learnt a bit more about the differences in micro controllers, that they all perform the same functionality (reading from GPIO pins or the USB and then performing outputs via the pins).

Now I was more confident with what these pins actually did I moved on to actually putting my microprocessor in.

Stage 3: (Put the microprocessor in):

To find the schematics for this microprocessor I went ahead and downloaded the OPL library that was linked in the Hack Club Guide.

After looking through the symbols I went looking for the RP2040 and was surprised to find 2 different footprints:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/39ad2b0ae6c536f60c8032e9350ee07fdec9a59a7e20e510dc71d1f66e82ce0f.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/afa458877435ee67e1d88a8d1a4af9c1277574a0755bcc52d139cff3d0b31d01.png)

Because I did not know what made this different to a normal RP2040 I went and asked AI what the difference was between these XIAO RP2040 SMD and DIP.

I learnt from this that the SMD or DIP ending were both the same microprocessor, just in different forms. The SMD was meant for soldering onto PCBs whereas the DIP was designed to be put together with breadboard circuits.

Because I was putting this on KICAD and planned to build a circuitboard using this I reckon that the SMD was the microprocessor I wanted.

At this point I became quite confused, if I were to simply buy a module for the modules anyway, I would not need to build a circuit board. All I would really need was to buy a XIAO RP2040 and plug in the components normally and from there I would already be able to develop the idea with programming. Therefore i would not need to build a PCB at all or do any routing.

I will take time to think of what to do next.

However, considering the size I was very unsure of why I would even make a PCB for this, the MAX7219 Module already had its own pcb and I would only end up plugging in the pcb to a microcontorller, in this case a XIAO RP2040.

I then realised what the purpose of the PCB was for:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/868e3426fd6b99ea5497c80106212c149d6f65a373b94c8f41d04dba67781f03.png)

Instead I was building this PCB in KiCad to make the Ports easier to access, rather than soldering directly onto the LEDs I could make a port to the microcontroller.

I the learnt that there was a difference between connectors and ports and learnt what a connector was meant to look like:

The guide now makes a lot more sense and gave me much more understanding of what I was building and how.

### 2026-10-30: At first I was figuring out whether to use the XIAO RP2040 schematic that I had from other hackclub kicad schematics.

**1h**

At first I was figuring out whether to use the XIAO RP2040 schematic that I had from other hackclub kicad schematics.

The two different options were:

 - The RP2040 DIP
 - Or the RP2040 SMD

The annoying thing was that both of these had a different number of pins:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/d4e4fa4d283f67f728538c0f7c96ffb6bb25d992656af9c14219fb0a70d26d48.png)

Because I did not know what to do at this point I went and checked with AI what made these different.

AI had told me that the smd was better suited for direct soldering whereas DIP was suited for bread boards but also warned me that the schematic for the XIAO RP2040 DIP was not according to the spec it had and recognised that it might be a third party schematic. It also told me to use the schematic that was safer which was the RP2040 SMD which I had got via the hackclub guide.

This led me to then use this SMD version.

I also had to check while doing this that the RP2040 I had found on Alibaba was a SMD

I then checked via AI whether this made any sense where I learnt what I was actually doing.

DIP and SMD only described how things were mounted and added to a printed circuit board.

DIP described that the component was mounted via male to female headers whereas SMD was soldered on. Because the guide had told me to use the SMD and I had no reliable version for the DIP, I thought it just easier to use the SMD version.

Now I knew what was happening finally so time to build the microcontroller section:

Stage 1)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/c0d616821eae5bd75401c367ed5a04a047f8dac98a17279496a4719e2b4cbd6d.png)

I have now put my microcontroller on, this is the SMD and the one I got from the library

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/e7987af3cf10d50114bc237f3267ab93e35e9d58c643ebab1c52d018d94dda84.png)

I have connected the power cables (+5v, GND) and added the netting labels which make up my SPI (DIN, CLK and CS)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/f08b779b5a713b7c7645f68a20578193d2542c0eb9b8d4cf8a532ec0323cf457.png)

I now added the capacitor to prevent random fluctuations in power.

I then realised a mistake.

According to the guide I had to put the pins with specific functionality, why I am going to find out but for now I just had to do that and fix it:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/70f909e67ecd012d0fe3ef74da03d9af95ecba55a63d121c6278dadaa0256e72.png)

I realised an even bigger mistake though. My pins for the connector had grounded the power and also didnt have a ground, therefore the system wouldn't actually work.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/d4301f2b8412d623c5ca0c0647f89ecf929365d6052c94d51a8bd5e3245f6b67.png)

This finally works.

I then went and learnt what the MOSI and SCK means for pin headings and why they were in specific GPIOs

The reason is that there is specific hardware that means it is easier for hardware communication on those 2 pins, which are able to control the clock (SCK) and direct what instructions are made (MOSI)

I then had to add the net labels to the connectors. Before I did anything major I thought it best to check what was done in the actual MAX7219 I was planning to buy.

After checking all the guides online, they all concurred with what was being said on the guide and looked like the MAX7219 I was planning to buy.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/d1929517f0d4956e530bd15bbf0153a6e8af4db2ff2ac4aab19caf0e60937418.png)

This is the complete schematic so far.

I then had a brief look at the checks below

Stage 2:(Check the Schematic):

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/e5f0f18225b8a07096846bd621025c6c09a4df022ba7198905c99f591d7a52b7.png)

 1) I had already assigned +5v to the power supply and therefore when going into the next system I already had the 5v I needed
 2)  I did not know what power budget was and how it related to current. I therefore asked AI what power budget was and how to calculate it and what it would mean in this case. It told me to add the current together from all modules:

Plan for 320mA for each module fully lit in practice. If I were to try use 4 modules I would need 4 * 320mA = 1280mA  = 1.28A

150 * 4 = 600mA if I were to use the general use in practice and this is still less current that I may be able to provide.

This was way above the 500mA that was provided from the USB power supply. I was originally concerned about this but I would consider these factor tomorrow.

### 2026-10-31: Today I started off checking my schematic made sense using the checklist from yesterday:

**0.83h**

Today I started off checking my schematic made sense using the checklist from yesterday:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/4ae7dbc338b5c13c99362a5c47548b1970884f86fb4f78e998c80ea73148a011.png)

1) I already checked from yesterday but I am supplying 5v to the system so I knew that was find

2) The power budget I had to learn yesterday which was the amount of current that went through each module. Currently (current haha), I would need to have 320mA * 4 = 1200 + 80 mA = 1280mA for the system to be full lit up

Even though this would mean I could just supply less current, I did want to have the flexibility in brightness so I would need to 5v 2A power supply. How I would add this I would not know or I could just keep this on low brightness.

3) Logic high: I had researched yesterday what a logic high was and found out this was the minimum voltage in a system that could be unambiguously detremined as on or off. For the system I would need 3.5v for a logic high whereas I currently from the RP2040 only able to supply 3.3v

4) Because I would be using a ready made module for the project this condition would be of no concern to me

5) Because I was just developing a micrcontroller for this, I would not need to worry about modelling the PCB

Fixes:
3) To account for logical high errors I could use a level shifter so I followed the guide and added one in:

I started to get the levelers and putting the schematic in however when I opened it there was no GND or VCC and I did not know what was happening:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/c00bb3428b5ef6e2302a47f07edd47985c5ce6375328a200e80ef1425f00fe32.png) (Onw on the right)

After asking AI what happened to the rest of the pins, I was able to find out that this was simply the wrong form of the 74AHCT125 and I needed the U2E component which I had literally no idea you could do.

Thankfully I was able to add it in and now power it

I then asked AI why were these chips in different components and why were they not all shown at the same time. I then learnt that it was just for ease of use, that it would mean less components seem to be everywhere and if I made sure that the same cmponent had the same unit name it was fine.

I now needed to add the rest of the Buffers in the circuit.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/5f6eb368930ff894bff3e1dc952a696b77f29b93447755f06cbc704a286c4828.png)

I added the buffers and connected them to ground. Out of curiosity I went and researched what the OE pins actually meant and what I was actually doing with them. I learnt that these Pins just described whether the input would actually go through to the output as if unplugging and plugging back in the input.

Applying a voltage accross would stop the flow and 0v would let the flow move. Because we have no reason to not let the flow through we just tie it to ground (0v) and let it always flow.

Because I didn't want to directly connect the microcontroller to the buffers and not use netting I made new ones:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/6c8f0506a2371430881705e1fcb8471c84a2390e954ac478235c4eaaae8a72ad.png)

I also needed to add a capacitor anyway:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/d7aec9e1029d04394d84d3e9243e13f384d7788261b7d5b01fd1f18558f961d1.png)
